Design a 10-14 minute video lesson. Start with a clear analogy for interfaces (e.g., a standard plug socket for different appliances). Introduce ABCs with a live coding demo of `DataSource` and its concrete implementations, showing the `TypeError` when abstract methods are missed. Explain `isinstance` and `issubclass` behavior. Transition to Protocols, explaining the shift from nominal to structural subtyping. Live-code the `Readable` protocol example, emphasizing how static type checkers benefit. Use side-by-side code blocks to compare ABCs and Protocols for the same conceptual interface. Include a quiz question after each major concept (ABCs, Protocols) to reinforce understanding. Use visual cues like 'contract' diagrams for ABCs and 'duck' icons for protocols.

screens.title: Abstract Base Classes (ABCs) and Protocols
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will formalize the idea of an interface in Python. You already know Python’s duck typing, where behavior matters more than inheritance. Here we contrast two ways to express that behavior. First, Abstract Base Classes let you declare a contract that concrete subclasses must implement. That enforces method presence at class-definition time and is useful when you control the class hierarchy. Second, Protocols express the same intent as duck typing but in a way that a static type checker can verify. Protocols let unrelated classes be treated as conforming simply by providing required methods. Throughout this chapter you will see concrete code examples that show DataSource and Readable interfaces, a hands-on activity building a LogFormatter ABC and a LogSender Protocol, and a short quiz-style question on Shape and area. By the end you will know when to prefer nominal subtyping for strict runtime enforcement and when to prefer structural subtyping for flexible, statically checked duck typing. Think of an electrical socket: ABCs give you a socket that only accepts plugs explicitly labelled to fit, while Protocols let any plug that matches the shape and pins be used and checked by a separate inspector.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › ABCs & Protocols Overview
Abstract Base Classes and Protocols
Formalize interfaces: enforce contracts or describe behavior for static checks.

Why this matters: as systems grow, implicit duck typing can let errors creep in. ABCs give runtime enforcement; Protocols give readable, checkable behavior without inheritance.

You'll see code examples, a live-style walkthrough, and a hands-on starter for a logging interface that practices both approaches.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next segment you will hone four practical skills that let you define and verify interfaces in Python. First, understand why Abstract Base Classes exist and how they let you declare firm contracts for subclasses. You will see concrete reasons this prevents runtime surprises. Second, implement ABCs using the abc module: inherit from the ABC base, mark methods with the abstract decorator, and combine abstractmethod with property for abstract attributes. Third, learn how to register or recognize virtual subclasses so third-party classes can be treated as implementing an interface without changing their source. Finally, begin using typing. Protocol to define structural interfaces that static tools like MyPy can check. Each objective includes a quick mnemonic or visual hint so you remember when to prefer strict runtime enforcement versus flexible structural checks. By practicing these skills you will write code that communicates design intent and helps collaborators and tools catch mismatches earlier.

screens.title: Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on skills you will practice. First, combine @property with @abstractmethod to declare abstract properties correctly; this avoids the deprecated abstractproperty and keeps property semantics intact. Second, learn to use isinstance and issubclass checks both with ABCs and, when enabled, with Protocols annotated with runtime_checkable. That gives you tools to validate objects at runtime. Third, practice creating simple concrete implementations that satisfy an ABC and observe the TypeError when you omit required methods. Observing this failure mode is an important learning step. Fourth, apply Protocols to allow third-party or existing classes to be accepted by your APIs without changing their base classes. These skills will help you design clearer APIs, catch mistakes earlier, and choose the right balance between strict enforcement and flexible behavior-based designs.

screens.title: Why formal interfaces? A clear analogy
screens.narratorSegment: Let's start with a simple analogy that clarifies why formal interfaces matter. Imagine a standard electrical socket in a building. A plug designed for that socket fits and will work safely. If any plug could be shoved in without checks, devices might fail or cause harm. In software, the 'socket' is your A P I contract and the 'plug' is an object passed into a function. Abstract Base Classes let you require that the plug explicitly declares it fits the socket by inheriting from a base type. That gives immediate, clear diagnostic errors when a class does not implement required members. Protocols, in contrast, are like a skilled inspector who examines a plug's pins and wiring and accepts it if it matches the expected shape. Protocols don't require explicit inheritance; they accept any object matching the shape. A common misconception is that duck typing is always sufficient. It often works for small scripts, but in larger projects the lack of explicit contracts can hide misspelled method names or incompatible signatures until a runtime error. Today we'll use both approaches: use ABCs when you control the hierarchy and need runtime enforcement; use Protocols when you need flexible, static checks for third-party or loose types. Reflect: which approach would you pick for a public framework A P I versus an internal utility class?

keyIdea.title: Analogy
keyIdea.text: Socket vs inspector: ABCs demand explicit inheritance; Protocols accept matching behavior without inheritance.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Interface Analogy
Socket vs Inspector
Use this mental model to choose a strategy. Abstractions protect large systems by making expectations explicit.
ABCs — socket
Require explicit fit via inheritance. Fail fast when methods are missing.
Protocols — inspector
Accept objects that match required methods, without changing their base classes.
Duck typing
Flexible but lacks static guarantees; can be paired with Protocols for safety.
Concrete considerations
  • ABCs fit when you control the class hierarchy or build a framework that requires guaranteed implementations.
  • Protocols are best when you need to accept existing classes or you prefer static analysis without altering inheritance.
  • Misconception: a Protocol is a runtime replacement for ABCs. It is primarily a static tool unless decorated with runtime_checkable.
Key Takeaway

Choose ABCs for strict runtime enforcement. Use Protocols when you want behavior-based acceptance and static checking.

screens.title: Creating an ABC: the DataSource example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a canonical ABC example: DataSource. The DataSource class inherits from abc. ABC and declares three abstract members: read_data, write_data, and an abstract property is_connected. The abstractmethod decorator marks methods that concrete subclasses must implement, and combining property with abstractmethod defines required properties correctly. Practically, this means that attempting to define a subclass that omits any of these members will either leave the subclass abstract or cause a TypeError when you try to instantiate a non-abstract class. The example shows FileSource implementing the required methods and returning True for is_connected, while DatabaseSource adapts the signatures for database usage and returns False for is_connected to indicate connection management. A common misconception is that abstract methods provide implementation; they do not. They only declare intent and enforce that concrete classes provide real behavior. The concrete example helps you understand how isinstance and issubclass reflect inheritance: FileSource instances are instances of DataSource because they inherit and implement the contract. Consider what would happen if you accidentally misspelled read_data in a subclass; the ABC machinery will prevent instantiation and force you to correct the contract violation.

keyIdea.title: ABC pattern
keyIdea.text: Use abc.ABC and @abstractmethod to declare required methods and properties that subclasses must implement.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › DataSource ABC
Code example
import abc

class DataSource(abc.ABC):
  @abc.abstractmethod
  def read_data(self, path):
    """Reads data from the specified path."""
    pass

  @abc.abstractmethod
  def write_data(self, path, data):
    """Writes data to the specified path."""
    pass

  @property
  @abc.abstractmethod
  def is_connected(self):
    """Returns True if the data source is connected."""
    pass

class FileSource(DataSource):
  def read_data(self, path):
    print(f"Reading from file: {path}")
    return f"Data from {path}"

  def write_data(self, path, data):
    print(f"Writing '{data}' to file: {path}")

  @property
  def is_connected(self):
    return True
Explanation & notes
  • The abstract base prevents instantiation if required methods are missing. This catches errors early.
  • Abstract properties combine @property and @abstractmethod so attribute-style access remains consistent.
  • Concrete subclasses must match expected signatures; mismatches lead to the class remaining abstract or instantiation errors.
Common mistake

Forgetting to implement an abstract member or misspelling its name will leave the subclass abstract.

Key Takeaway

ABCs declare required behavior and force concrete classes to provide real implementations before use.

screens.title: Instantiating and errors: what goes wrong
screens.narratorSegment: A common learning moment is seeing a TypeError when you define or instantiate a subclass that fails to satisfy an ABC. This happens because the class system enforces that any concrete subclass implement all abstract methods. If you forget to implement one, the subclass remains abstract or Python raises a TypeError when the class is created or when instantiation is attempted. To debug, compare the abstract method names and signatures in the base class with your subclass. Misspellings or wrong parameter lists are the usual culprits. Another pattern is to intentionally create an abstract intermediary class by declaring its own abstract methods. That is valid: an abstract subclass can add abstract members and remain abstract. For example, a Polygon class that inherits Shape and adds num_sides as an abstract method is still abstract and will not raise TypeError at definition time. A misconception is thinking TypeError always means a runtime call failed; here it signals incomplete class construction. Always inspect class definitions and use tools or quick test instantiation to validate that your concrete classes are instantiable. Instantiating and errors: what goes wrong means typeerror often indicates an unimplemented abstract member or mismatched signature; inspect definitions and fix the contract violation.. In practical terms, why typeerror appears and how to debug missing abstract members. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Debug tip
keyIdea.text: TypeError often indicates an unimplemented abstract member or mismatched signature; inspect definitions and fix the contract violation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › TypeError & Debugging
Common scenarios
Forgot to implement an abstract method
You will see a TypeError at class definition or when instantiating. Fix by adding the missing method.
Misspelled or wrong signature
A method with the wrong name or parameters won't satisfy the abstract requirement. Match name and signature precisely.
Intentionally abstract subclasses
A subclass can remain abstract by introducing its own abstract members; this is valid design and does not raise TypeError at definition.
Quick debugging checklist
  1. Compare abstract method names and parameters against the subclass.
  2. Try a minimal instantiation test to confirm the error reproduces.
  3. Consider whether the subclass should be abstract or concrete; add @abstractmethod if it should remain abstract.
Misconception

TypeError is not always a runtime call failure; it often signals incomplete class implementation and helps you find design gaps early.

Key Takeaway

Treat TypeError as a helpful signal that your contract is unsatisfied; fix method names or implement the missing behavior.

screens.title: Virtual subclasses and collections.abc
screens.narratorSegment: Virtual subclasses provide a way to treat a class as if it were a subclass of an ABC without changing its inheritance. This is handy when you use third-party classes that already implement the necessary methods but you cannot modify their base class. The collections. abc module offers many ABCs like Sized, Iterable, Mapping, and Sequence. Some ABCs perform structural checks by inspecting methods such as len, and so an object can be treated as that ABC if it provides the required dunder methods. You can also explicitly register a class with an ABC using ABC. register, which makes isinstance and issubclass treat that class as a subclass. The provided example shows MyCustomCollection implementing len and getitem and being recognized by Sized because Sized checks for len. Another example registers AnotherSizedObject with Sized so isinstance returns True. A misconception is registering too freely: registration only affects runtime subclass checks and does not magically add missing methods. Use registration to document intent and to enable isinstance-based code paths, but test behavior as well. Virtual subclasses and collections.abc means register third-party or custom types with abcs to enable isinstance and issubclass checks without modifying their inheritance.. In practical terms, recognize and register classes that behave like built-in container types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Virtual subclassing
keyIdea.text: Register third-party or custom types with ABCs to enable isinstance and issubclass checks without modifying their inheritance.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Virtual Subclasses
Example: Sized recognition
from collections.abc import Sized

class MyCustomCollection:
  def __init__(self, items):
    self._items = list(items)
  def __len__(self):
    return len(self._items)
  def __getitem__(self, index):
    return self._items[index]

print(isinstance(MyCustomCollection([1,2,3]), Sized))  # True
Notes and caution
  • Recognition can be implicit when an ABC inspects expected methods, or explicit via register().
  • Registration affects type checks, not object behavior. The object must implement required methods to behave correctly.
  • Use registration to document that a class should be accepted by APIs expecting the ABC.
Pro tip

Prefer implicit structural checks when available; register only when you need explicit isinstance behavior for readability or compatibility.

screens.title: Introducing Protocols: Readable example
screens.narratorSegment: Protocols express structural subtyping: you define the shape of an interface by listing required methods and attributes. The Readable protocol in our source defines a read method returning a string. Any class that provides a read method matching that signature implicitly conforms to Readable. If you decorate the protocol with runtime_checkable, you also gain runtime isinstance checks. The chapter example shows FileReader and NetworkStream both providing read and being accepted. BadReader, which provides get_data instead, does not conform and a static type checker would flag passing it to a function that expects Readable. Protocols let you express duck typing explicitly so tools like MyPy can warn you before runtime. Important: Protocols do not alter inheritance or object behavior; they are a typing construct. Use them when you want flexible acceptance of objects that share behavior, especially across existing libraries you cannot change. Introducing Protocols: Readable example means use protocols to declare behavior by shape; classes conform by providing required methods, enabling static analysis and optional runtime checks.. In practical terms, define a protocol to express a read() method and use it in an api. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Protocol pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Protocols to declare behavior by shape; classes conform by providing required methods, enabling static analysis and optional runtime checks.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Readable Protocol
Protocol code
from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable

@runtime_checkable
class Readable(Protocol):
  def read(self) -> str:
    ...

class FileReader:
  def read(self) -> str:
    return "Content from file."

class BadReader:
  def get_data(self) -> str:
    return "Wrong method name."

def process_readable(reader: Readable):
  print(reader.read())
Explanation
  • Readable is a Protocol declaring a read method. Any class with a matching method conforms by shape.
  • @runtime_checkable enables isinstance checks at runtime, but Protocols primarily help static type checkers.
  • A class that does not provide read will not conform and will be flagged by a type checker when used where Readable is expected.
Key Takeaway

Protocols make duck typing explicit and checkable, improving readability and tooling support without changing runtime inheritance.

screens.title: Nominal vs Structural subtyping
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between ABCs and Protocols depends on control, enforcement needs, and tooling. Nominal subtyping, provided by ABCs, requires explicit inheritance. Use it when you own the class hierarchy and want runtime guarantees that subclasses implement required members. Structural subtyping, provided by Protocols, accepts any object that matches the expected shape. Use Protocols when you want to accept existing or third-party classes without changing their base classes. A useful rule of thumb: pick ABCs for frameworks and strict APIs where you want to enforce implementation. Pick Protocols for libraries and utilities that should interoperate with many types and where static checkers can provide early warnings. A common misconception is that Protocols eliminate the need for tests. They help catch mismatches in signatures, but Protocols do not verify runtime behavior or side effects. Combine them: you can define a Protocol for flexible typing, and an ABC when a strict runtime contract is essential. Which property of your A P I makes you prefer one over the other: control or flexibility? Nominal vs Structural subtyping means use abcs when you need strict runtime enforcement; use protocols when you prefer flexible, statically checkable behavior.. In practical terms, when to choose abcs or protocols. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Nominal vs Structural
Side-by-side
ABCs (Nominal)
Require inheritance; enforce at runtime; good for frameworks and strict APIs.
Protocols (Structural)
Accept any object by shape; good for libraries and static checks; flexible with third-party code.
Misconception
Protocols replace testing. They do not — they complement static checks but cannot validate runtime side effects or resource behavior.
Decision checklist
  • Do you control the type hierarchy? Prefer ABCs for enforcement.
  • Do you need to accept many existing types? Prefer Protocols for flexibility.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Activity Solution
Solution sketch
class SimpleFormatter(LogFormatter):
  def format_record(self, record: dict) -> str:
    return f"{record['level']}: {record['message']} @ {record['timestamp']}"

class ConsoleSender:
  def send_log(self, formatted_message: str):
    print(f"Console: {formatted_message}")

class NetworkSender:
  def send_log(self, formatted_message: str):
    print(f"Network: Sending '{formatted_message}' over network.")
Why this design works
  • Formatters produce a single string output so senders have a stable input contract.
  • Senders implement a single responsibility: transmit the formatted message by their chosen transport.
  • Using an ABC for formatters enforces that formatting exists. Using a Protocol for senders allows flexible acceptance of varied transports.

screens.title: Assessment: Shape example and reasoning
screens.narratorSegment: This assessment question helps you reason about abstract classes and when a class definition produces a TypeError. The Shape example asks which subclasses will not raise a TypeError at definition time. The safe answers are classes that either implement the abstract method or remain abstract themselves by adding their own abstract methods. For instance, Triangle implements area and is concrete, so it will not raise a TypeError at definition. Polygon declares another abstract method and remains abstract; that's allowed. Circle and Square that inherit but fail to implement area and are not decorated as abstract will cause TypeError at definition time because a concrete class claims to implement the base but omits required members. A common misconception is that TypeError only appears when you instantiate a class. In this context Python can raise it at class creation/definition time to prevent creation of a concrete type that violates an interface. When answering such questions, check whether each subclass implements all abstract methods or itself declares abstract members. This habit will make reasoning about ABCs reliable in tests and in design reviews.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will formalize the idea of an interface in Python. You already know Python’s duck typing, where behavior matters more than inheritance. Here we contrast two ways to express that behavior. First, Abstract Base Classes let you declare a contract that concrete subclasses must implement. That enforces method presence at class-definition time and is useful when you control the class hierarchy. Second, Protocols express the same intent as duck typing but in a way that a static type checker can verify. Protocols let unrelated classes be treated as conforming simply by providing required methods. Throughout this chapter you will see concrete code examples that show DataSource and Readable interfaces, a hands-on activity building a LogFormatter ABC and a LogSender Protocol, and a short quiz-style question on Shape and area. By the end you will know when to prefer nominal subtyping for strict runtime enforcement and when to prefer structural subtyping for flexible, statically checked duck typing. Think of an electrical socket: ABCs give you a socket that only accepts plugs explicitly labelled to fit, while Protocols let any plug that matches the shape and pins be used and checked by a separate inspector.

Over the next segment you will hone four practical skills that let you define and verify interfaces in Python. First, understand why Abstract Base Classes exist and how they let you declare firm contracts for subclasses. You will see concrete reasons this prevents runtime surprises. Second, implement ABCs using the abc module: inherit from the ABC base, mark methods with the abstract decorator, and combine abstractmethod with property for abstract attributes. Third, learn how to register or recognize virtual subclasses so third-party classes can be treated as implementing an interface without changing their source. Finally, begin using typing. Protocol to define structural interfaces that static tools like MyPy can check. Each objective includes a quick mnemonic or visual hint so you remember when to prefer strict runtime enforcement versus flexible structural checks. By practicing these skills you will write code that communicates design intent and helps collaborators and tools catch mismatches earlier.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on skills you will practice. First, combine @property with @abstractmethod to declare abstract properties correctly; this avoids the deprecated abstractproperty and keeps property semantics intact. Second, learn to use isinstance and issubclass checks both with ABCs and, when enabled, with Protocols annotated with runtime_checkable. That gives you tools to validate objects at runtime. Third, practice creating simple concrete implementations that satisfy an ABC and observe the TypeError when you omit required methods. Observing this failure mode is an important learning step. Fourth, apply Protocols to allow third-party or existing classes to be accepted by your APIs without changing their base classes. These skills will help you design clearer APIs, catch mistakes earlier, and choose the right balance between strict enforcement and flexible behavior-based designs.

Let's start with a simple analogy that clarifies why formal interfaces matter. Imagine a standard electrical socket in a building. A plug designed for that socket fits and will work safely. If any plug could be shoved in without checks, devices might fail or cause harm. In software, the 'socket' is your A P I contract and the 'plug' is an object passed into a function. Abstract Base Classes let you require that the plug explicitly declares it fits the socket by inheriting from a base type. That gives immediate, clear diagnostic errors when a class does not implement required members. Protocols, in contrast, are like a skilled inspector who examines a plug's pins and wiring and accepts it if it matches the expected shape. Protocols don't require explicit inheritance; they accept any object matching the shape. A common misconception is that duck typing is always sufficient. It often works for small scripts, but in larger projects the lack of explicit contracts can hide misspelled method names or incompatible signatures until a runtime error. Today we'll use both approaches: use ABCs when you control the hierarchy and need runtime enforcement; use Protocols when you need flexible, static checks for third-party or loose types. Reflect: which approach would you pick for a public framework A P I versus an internal utility class?

Let's walk through a canonical ABC example: DataSource. The DataSource class inherits from abc. ABC and declares three abstract members: read_data, write_data, and an abstract property is_connected. The abstractmethod decorator marks methods that concrete subclasses must implement, and combining property with abstractmethod defines required properties correctly. Practically, this means that attempting to define a subclass that omits any of these members will either leave the subclass abstract or cause a TypeError when you try to instantiate a non-abstract class. The example shows FileSource implementing the required methods and returning True for is_connected, while DatabaseSource adapts the signatures for database usage and returns False for is_connected to indicate connection management. A common misconception is that abstract methods provide implementation; they do not. They only declare intent and enforce that concrete classes provide real behavior. The concrete example helps you understand how isinstance and issubclass reflect inheritance: FileSource instances are instances of DataSource because they inherit and implement the contract. Consider what would happen if you accidentally misspelled read_data in a subclass; the ABC machinery will prevent instantiation and force you to correct the contract violation.

A common learning moment is seeing a TypeError when you define or instantiate a subclass that fails to satisfy an ABC. This happens because the class system enforces that any concrete subclass implement all abstract methods. If you forget to implement one, the subclass remains abstract or Python raises a TypeError when the class is created or when instantiation is attempted. To debug, compare the abstract method names and signatures in the base class with your subclass. Misspellings or wrong parameter lists are the usual culprits. Another pattern is to intentionally create an abstract intermediary class by declaring its own abstract methods. That is valid: an abstract subclass can add abstract members and remain abstract. For example, a Polygon class that inherits Shape and adds num_sides as an abstract method is still abstract and will not raise TypeError at definition time. A misconception is thinking TypeError always means a runtime call failed; here it signals incomplete class construction. Always inspect class definitions and use tools or quick test instantiation to validate that your concrete classes are instantiable. Instantiating and errors: what goes wrong means typeerror often indicates an unimplemented abstract member or mismatched signature; inspect definitions and fix the contract violation.. In practical terms, why typeerror appears and how to debug missing abstract members. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Virtual subclasses provide a way to treat a class as if it were a subclass of an ABC without changing its inheritance. This is handy when you use third-party classes that already implement the necessary methods but you cannot modify their base class. The collections. abc module offers many ABCs like Sized, Iterable, Mapping, and Sequence. Some ABCs perform structural checks by inspecting methods such as len, and so an object can be treated as that ABC if it provides the required dunder methods. You can also explicitly register a class with an ABC using ABC. register, which makes isinstance and issubclass treat that class as a subclass. The provided example shows MyCustomCollection implementing len and getitem and being recognized by Sized because Sized checks for len. Another example registers AnotherSizedObject with Sized so isinstance returns True. A misconception is registering too freely: registration only affects runtime subclass checks and does not magically add missing methods. Use registration to document intent and to enable isinstance-based code paths, but test behavior as well. Virtual subclasses and collections.abc means register third-party or custom types with abcs to enable isinstance and issubclass checks without modifying their inheritance.. In practical terms, recognize and register classes that behave like built-in container types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Protocols express structural subtyping: you define the shape of an interface by listing required methods and attributes. The Readable protocol in our source defines a read method returning a string. Any class that provides a read method matching that signature implicitly conforms to Readable. If you decorate the protocol with runtime_checkable, you also gain runtime isinstance checks. The chapter example shows FileReader and NetworkStream both providing read and being accepted. BadReader, which provides get_data instead, does not conform and a static type checker would flag passing it to a function that expects Readable. Protocols let you express duck typing explicitly so tools like MyPy can warn you before runtime. Important: Protocols do not alter inheritance or object behavior; they are a typing construct. Use them when you want flexible acceptance of objects that share behavior, especially across existing libraries you cannot change. Introducing Protocols: Readable example means use protocols to declare behavior by shape; classes conform by providing required methods, enabling static analysis and optional runtime checks.. In practical terms, define a protocol to express a read() method and use it in an api. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing between ABCs and Protocols depends on control, enforcement needs, and tooling. Nominal subtyping, provided by ABCs, requires explicit inheritance. Use it when you own the class hierarchy and want runtime guarantees that subclasses implement required members. Structural subtyping, provided by Protocols, accepts any object that matches the expected shape. Use Protocols when you want to accept existing or third-party classes without changing their base classes. A useful rule of thumb: pick ABCs for frameworks and strict APIs where you want to enforce implementation. Pick Protocols for libraries and utilities that should interoperate with many types and where static checkers can provide early warnings. A common misconception is that Protocols eliminate the need for tests. They help catch mismatches in signatures, but Protocols do not verify runtime behavior or side effects. Combine them: you can define a Protocol for flexible typing, and an ABC when a strict runtime contract is essential.
